title: Becoming a Manager Is Only Half the Job
excerpt: A personal reflection on the difference between managing people and leading them.
content:
When you first become a manager, it can feel like you've reached a destination. You've done well in your career, you've shown you're capable, and someone has decided you're ready to take responsibility for other people. It's a big step, and for a lot of people it's something they've been working towards for years.

I think it's really the start of something much bigger. I've come to realise there are two sides to the job. The management side is the one we're probably all familiar with: 1:1s, feedback, objectives, performance, career development, future plans and making sure people know what's expected of them. All of that is important, and a team without good management can quickly become confused and frustrated.

The other side is harder to define, and that's leadership. I think it's possible to be a perfectly competent manager without being a great leader.

## Management and leadership aren't the same thing

Management is relatively easy to describe because there are tangible things you can do. You can hold regular 1:1s and make sure objectives are clear. You can give people feedback, help them think about their development, talk about performance and plan where someone wants to go in their career. These things are fundamental to being a good manager.

Leadership is much less tangible. It's about the person you are while you're doing all of that. Do people trust and respect you? Do they feel comfortable coming to you when something has gone wrong? Do they believe you have their interests at heart? When things get difficult, does your involvement reassure people or worry them more?

And perhaps the biggest question: would people choose to follow you if they didn't have to?

That's where the distinction gets interesting. Management comes with a job title and leadership doesn't. You can tell somebody what to do because you're their manager, but a position of authority can't make anyone respect you, trust you or believe in what you're trying to achieve. That has to be earned.

## Leadership becomes most obvious when things go wrong

It's relatively easy to look like a good leader when everything is going well. The project is on track, the team is performing, everyone gets along and you're hitting your targets. Most people feel pretty good about their manager in those circumstances.

The real test comes when things aren't going well. A project has gone badly. Someone has made a significant mistake. There's pressure from above, or two people in your team aren't getting along, or a decision you made turns out to be the wrong one. At that point there aren't any easy answers, and what counts is how you respond.

Do you look for someone to blame, or take responsibility? Do you protect yourself, or stand in front of your team? Do you pretend you know exactly what to do, or are you comfortable saying, *"I'm not sure, let's work it out together"*?

People remember those moments. Over time they build your reputation far more than a perfectly run 1:1 or a hit objective, because people learn what you're like when things get difficult: whether they can rely on you, whether you'll support them and whether you'll be honest with them.

## What happens when you leave?

There's another way of thinking about leadership that I find quite useful.

Imagine you've been at a company for five years and decide it's time to move on. You've managed a team, helped people develop, worked on projects and had all the usual ups and downs that come with being somewhere for a long time.

The company will carry on, of course. Someone else will take over the team and the work will continue. But what do the people you worked with say about you after you've gone?

Do they simply remember you as their manager? Or do they say things like *"I learned a huge amount from them"*, *"They helped me become a better version of myself"* or *"I'd happily work with them again"*? If you've really made an impact, someone might even say, *"Wherever they go next, I'd seriously consider following them."*

I think that's one of the things that separates a good manager from a great one. I don't mean building a little army that follows you from company to company. I mean earning enough trust and respect that people want to work with you again because of the experience they had. If people are better for having worked with you, that's a pretty good measure of leadership.

## You need both

I don't see management and leadership as competing ideas. You need both.

A great leader who can't manage can leave a team inspired but without direction. People might like them, but they may not understand what's expected of them or how they're supposed to develop.

Equally, someone can be an incredibly organised manager who runs excellent 1:1s, sets clear objectives and handles performance well, but never earns the trust or respect of their team. The team might function perfectly well, but people doing their jobs because they have to is different from people wanting to be part of something.

The managers I've admired most have had both sides. They can sit down with someone and have a difficult conversation about performance, help them work out what it takes to reach the next level, make hard decisions and give clear direction. They're also the person you want beside you when things get difficult: someone you trust, someone you look to when you don't know what to do, and someone who can make you believe that whatever the problem is, you'll figure it out together.

## So what should you focus on when you become a manager?

If you're stepping into management for the first time, learn the management stuff. Learn how to run good 1:1s, give useful feedback, set expectations, have difficult conversations and support people's development.

But don't stop there. Start thinking about the leader you want to become:

- How do you behave under pressure?
- Do you take responsibility when things go wrong, and give credit to others when they go right?
- Do people feel safe telling you that you're wrong?
- Are the people around you getting better because you're their manager?

And perhaps most importantly, what do you want people to say about you when you're no longer their manager?

I think that's the part that often gets missed when we talk about management. Becoming a manager gives you responsibility for a team, but influence over people only comes with the trust you build.

When you can manage people well and also become someone they genuinely trust, respect and want to follow, the job changes. You're running a team, and you're also helping people grow into colleagues who'll carry what they learned from you into whatever they do next.
